## Motivation

A manager has to choose one of a few actions without knowing which state of the world
will hold. Decision analysis starts by writing that down as a table: one row per
action, one column per state, and in each cell the outcome of taking that action when
that state holds. This vignette builds such a table with `DecisionAnalysis.jl`, attaches
a belief about the states, and finds the action with the largest expected outcome. It
also introduces the comparison that every vignette in this series makes: each action is
measured against doing nothing.

The currency is individuals. Outcomes are counted as the number of animals of the focal
species, never as money.

## The problem

Natterjack toads breed in shallow, temporary ponds on a dune system. Shallow ponds warm
quickly and hold few predators, but in a dry spring they dry out before the tadpoles
have metamorphosed. The manager can leave the ponds alone, deepen the existing ponds, or
dig new shallow scrapes. The outcome is the number of toadlets that leave the ponds this
year. Every toadlet counts as one individual.

The state of the world is the spring rainfall: dry, average or wet.

**All numbers in this vignette are illustrative.** They were chosen to make the
arithmetic easy to follow. They are not data and they are not estimates for any real
site.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))   # plot defaults and small tables, no analysis

actions = [:no_intervention, :deepen_ponds, :dig_scrapes, :deepen_and_dig]
states = [:dry, :average, :wet]
toadlets = [ 200 1200 2000     # no intervention: the ponds dry out in a dry spring
             900 1400 1500     # deeper ponds hold water, and in a wet spring hold predators
             300 1700 2400     # more shallow ponds: more habitat, the same drying risk
            1000 1800 2000]    # both at once
payoff = individuals_payoff(PayoffTable(actions, states, toadlets))
```

`PayoffTable(actions, states, Q)` stores `Q[a, θ]`, with rows for actions and columns
for states. Higher is better. `individuals_payoff` says what the utility is: the
payoff of an action in a state *is* the count of individuals, so the table of counts is
the payoff table (the function checks that no count is negative and returns it). A
`PayoffTable` displays itself as a table; nothing else is needed to print it.

The fourth action is the best or equal best in two of the three springs, but the site
has machinery for one kind of work this season, so it cannot be carried out. It stays in
the table and is excluded by a feasibility filter below.

## A belief about the states

The belief is a probability for each state. Here a dry spring has probability 3/10, an
average one 1/2 and a wet one 1/5 (illustrative). Writing them as rationals keeps
every later number exact.

```{julia}
belief = FiniteBelief(states, [3 // 10, 1 // 2, 1 // 5])
md_table(["state", "probability"],
         [[s, exact(p)] for (s, p) in zip(state_labels(belief), probabilities(belief))])
```

## The decision problem and its baseline

A `DecisionProblem` pairs the table with the belief. Two keywords matter here.

- `baseline` names the action that stands for no intervention, business as usual.
  Setting it changes no score and no choice. It adds the comparison with doing nothing.
- `feasible` filters the actions. Infeasible actions get no score and cannot be chosen.

```{julia}
problem = DecisionProblem(payoff, belief;
                          baseline=:no_intervention,
                          feasible=[:no_intervention, :deepen_ponds, :dig_scrapes])
feasible_actions(problem)
```

## Expected number of individuals

The expected number of toadlets under an action is the probability-weighted mean of its
row: the sum over states of probability times outcome. `aggregate` with the
`Expectation` aggregator computes it for every feasible action, and `decide` with
`MaxExpectedUtility` picks the largest.

```{julia}
result = decide(problem, MaxExpectedUtility())
```

```{julia}
first_choice(result), act_now_value(problem)
```

`decide` returns a `DecisionResult` with the scores, every chosen action (ties are all
listed) and the rule, and it displays as the table above. `first_choice` gives the single deterministic choice, and
`act_now_value` the expected number of toadlets under it.

As a check by hand, for digging scrapes:
3/10 × 300 + 1/2 × 1700 + 1/5 × 2400 = 90 + 850 + 480 = 1420.

## Gain over no intervention

The number that matters to a manager is how many more individuals an action yields than
doing nothing. `gain_over_baseline` gives that difference in every state, and
`expected_gain_over_baseline` its expectation.

```{julia}
gain_over_baseline(problem)
```

```{julia}
gain = expected_gain_over_baseline(problem)
md_table(["action", "expected gain over no intervention"],
         [[a, g] for (a, g) in zip(feasible_actions(problem), gain)])
```

The gain table shows something the expectations hide: an action can have a positive
expected gain and still lose individuals in some state. Deepening the ponds costs 500
toadlets in a wet spring.

```{julia}
G = gain_over_baseline(problem)
png_figure(grouped_bars(G.states, G.actions, permutedims(G.Q);
                        xlabel="spring rainfall", ylabel="gain in toadlets",
                        title="Gain over no intervention, by state (illustrative)"))
```

## When the state is known

If the spring were known in advance the belief would be a `PointBelief`, and the best
action would simply be the best cell in that column.

```{julia}
md_table(["known state", "best action", "toadlets"],
         [begin
              known = DecisionProblem(payoff, PointBelief(s);
                                      baseline=:no_intervention,
                                      feasible=feasible_actions(problem))
              [s, first_choice(decide(known, MaxExpectedUtility())),
               act_now_value(known)]
          end
          for s in states])
```

The best action differs between states, which is why the uncertainty matters. The
vignette on regret returns to this table of best actions.

## What the feasibility filter did

Without the filter the fourth action would have been chosen.

```{julia}
unfiltered = DecisionProblem(payoff, belief; baseline=:no_intervention)
first_choice(decide(unfiltered, MaxExpectedUtility())), act_now_value(unfiltered)
```

## What to take away

- A decision problem is a payoff table `Q[a, θ]` (rows are actions, columns are states),
  a belief about the states, and optionally a feasibility filter and a baseline.
- Outcomes here are counts of individuals. Higher is better.
- `aggregate(Expectation(), problem)` gives the expected count for each action and
  `decide(problem, MaxExpectedUtility())` the action that maximises it.
- Always name the no-intervention action as the `baseline`. `gain_over_baseline` and
  `expected_gain_over_baseline` then report what each action adds to doing nothing.
- An action with a positive expected gain can still do worse than no intervention in
  some states. Look at the gain table and not only at its expectation.
- Rational inputs give exact outputs.
